newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Minister renews warning of trouble in Russian army.
newsitem.headline: Minister renews warning of trouble in Russian army.

text.p: Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, under mounting pressure from his subordinates, said on Friday Russia's cash-strapped armed forces were on the brink of "uncontrollable developments."
In a speech to army veterans, Rodionov said a shortage of funds, appalling social conditions and poor maintenance were leading to a "severe crisis."

Interfax news agency quoted him as saying: "Russia's leadership and society should know that the chronic lack of funds is taking the armed forces to the brink of undesirable, and even uncontrollable, developments."
Rodionov's speech, which gave no details, coincided with a deadline set by a group of general staff officers, who threatened to use force if overdue wages were not paid.

The ultimatum, laid down in an open letter by the unnamed officers published last week, urged Rodionov to tackle those in the government it said were set on ruining Russia, which has Europe's biggest army, and surrendering it to the West.
"We have enough force to make these gentlemen abandon their plans," said the letter in the Nezavisimaya Gazeta daily.
There was no further word from the officers on Friday, but Rodionov's speech clearly reflected their concerns.
"If the 1997 defence budget is not changed, Russia may lose the armed forces as an integral and active state structure, with all the consequences which would follow that," he said.
Rodionov said the draft budget, rejected by parliament earlier this week, covered only one third of the minimum needs of the armed forces.

"There are lots of promises but so far little money," said a headline in Friday's defence ministry daily Krasnaya Zvezda (Red Star), which has published a string of stories cataloguing acute shortages of equipment and even food for the troops.
Russia's former national security chief, Alexander Lebed, sacked by President Boris Yeltsin last week, has said the 1.5 million-strong armed forces are on the brink of rebellion.
At the time, Rodionov rejected Lebed's predictions, saying the military was under control and there was no reason to expect any sort of mutiny.

Independent analysts took a similar line, but warned of a possible increase in crime and indiscipline due to plunging morale and financial desparation. A leaked CIA report this week said controls had even weakened over the nuclear arsenal.
In one recent example two new recruits shot dead four of their comrades in Russia's Far East this month and ran off with weapons and ammunition.

Earlier in the same region several soldiers were blown to bits when they tried to dismantle a missile, apparently to sell off the parts. Other reports record an increase in suicides and armed robberies in the army.

It is the second time Rodionov has called for urgent funding this month. On October 1, his cry for help brought an immediate response, an order from President Boris Yeltsin for a special meeting on army financing and new emphasis on reforms.
But while the ministry has managed to squeeze more money out of the government, it clearly feels it is not enough to appease those who are anyway stung by the army's lack of prestige.
Rodionov told the veterans he strongly supported the idea of reforming the huge and largely ineffective armed forces which Russia inherited from the now-defunct Soviet Union.

"Russia needs mobile, combat-ready and technically equipped armed forces whose power should be well known to any potential enemy," he said in a clear effort to win the support of those in the military who oppose the cutbacks reforms would involve.
During his re-election campaign, Yeltsin announced plans to turn Russia's conscript army into a professional force by the year 2000, but analysts say this is highly unlikely.
